idiom_name: try/finally around an async mutex (run-to-completion for sync code)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no lock primitive and no destructor, and ordinary code is single-threaded with run-to-completion, so most synchronous 'critical sections' are already atomic and need nothing. The pattern reappears where a task suspends: an await releases the event loop to other tasks, so an async critical section needs an async-aware mutex (a promise-queue library such as async-mutex, or a hand-rolled one), with the release in a finally and the acquisition awaited immediately before it. For genuine parallelism inside worker_threads, coordination moves to Atomics.wait/notify on a SharedArrayBuffer; across tabs and workers the Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request) holds a named lock for the duration of a callback and releases it automatically - the closest thing to a scope-bound guard in the platform.
pitfalls: A synchronous lock held across an await provides no mutual exclusion: the event loop runs other tasks between suspend and resume, so the guard must be async-aware.
try/finally is the only scope-exit hook: a missing finally leaks the mutex, and an un-awaited rejected promise hides both the failure and the release.
In worker_threads a thread cannot be blocked from JavaScript except by Atomics.wait, which is illegal on a browser main thread; do not build blocking locks around it in UI code.
Async mutexes are not reentrant: a nested acquisition by the same task (directly or via a helper) waits forever.
Unhandled rejections inside the critical section still run the finally, but the state may be half-updated - review what the mutual exclusion was actually protecting.
